stem_md:
There is a rectangular plot of size  $1 \times n$ . This has to be covered by three types of tiles - red, blue and black. The red tiles are of size  $1 \times 1$ , the blue tiles are of size  $1 \times 1$  and the black tiles are of size  $1 \times 2$ . Let  $t_n$  denote the number of ways this can be done. For example, clearly  $t_1 = 2$  because we can have either a red or a blue tile. Also  $t_2 = 5$  since we could have tiled the plot as: two red tiles, two blue tiles, a red tile on the left and a blue tile on the right, a blue tile on the left and a red tile on the right, or a single black tile. 

[list=a]
[*]Prove that  $t_{2n+1} = t_n(t_{n-1} + t_{n+1})$  for all  $n > 1$ .

[*]Prove that  $t_n = \sum_{d \ge 0} \binom{n-d}{d}2^{n-2d}$  for all  $n >0$ .
[/list]
Here, 
\[ \binom{m}{r} = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{m!}{r!(m-r)!}, &\text{ if  $0 \le r \le m$ ,} 
0, &\text{ otherwise}
\end{cases}\]
for integers  $m,r$ .
solution_md:
INMO 2018 hmm.
-----

(a): Sps  $t_{n}$  are the number of ways to tile the plot. 

Consider a plot of dimension  $1\times 2n+1$  for that, 

if the tile between  $n-1$  and  $n+2$  tile is not covered with black then there are  $t_{n} \cdot t_{n+1}$  ways to cover the plot. And if the tile between  $n-1$  and  $n+2$  is covered by a black tile then we notice first  $n-1$  tiles can be covered in  $t_{n-1}$  ways and rest tiles from  $n+2$  to  $2n+1$  can be covered in  $t_{n}$  ways hence in total we have  $t_{2n+1}=t_{n}(t_{n+1}+t_{n-1})$ .  $\square$ (b): Consider the plot is covered by  $d$  number of black tiles , then  $n-2d$  number of  $1 \times 1$  tiles are left to tile , Sps  $x_1$  number of  $1 \times 1$  tiles are before  $1$ st black tile ,  $x_{2}$  number of tiles are there between black tile  $1$  and black tiles  $2$  ,  $\cdots$  ,  $x_{d}$   be the number of tiles between  $d-1$  and  $d$ th black tile and  $x_{d+1}$  number of tiles after black tile  $d$  , 

so we have  $x_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{d+1}=n-2d$  we have to solve this equation in non-negative integers , solutions to this equation are  $\binom{n-2d+d+1-1}{d+1-1}=\binom{n-d}{d}$  and for each  $1\times 1$  tile we have  $2$  ways to fill it with a red tile or blue tile , hence   $$ t_{n}=\sum_{d \geqslant 0} \binom{n-d}{d} \cdot 2^{n-2d} $$  .  $\square$

candidates: (a) Note that if there were only one type of  $1 \times 1$  tile, then the recurrence would be the familiar Fibonacci recurrence  $t_{n+1}=t_n+t_{n-1}$ . However, the existence of the second type causes there to be a three-term recurrence, which is expressed in the form shown. A more rigorous method would be to show that each iteration is essentially twice the number of ways to partition into 1-2 sets, which also gives the recurrence.

For the term  $t_nt_{n-1}$  we first place first  $n$  tiles in first  $n$  blocks in  $t_n$  ways and then place a black tile covering the  $(n+1)th$  and  $(n+2)th$  block and then place the rest  $n-1$  in  $t_{n-1}$  ways.
    For the term  $t_nt_{n+1}$  we first place first  $n+1$  tiles in first  $n+1$  blocks in  $t_{n+1}$  ways and then place the rest  $n$  in  $t_n$  ways. 
    It is easy to check that this two cases are disjoint because if not i.e if there is some common tiling in this cases then since in the first case we have a black tile in  $(n+1)th$  place then so should we have in case two i.e the  $(n)th$  and  $(n+1)th$  block should be covered by a black tile and by the same logic so should be the  $(n+2)th$  and  $(n+3)th$  block and in this manner it is easy to see that the whole rectangular plot of size  $1 \times (2n+1)$  should only be covered with black tiles which is impossible due to parity.
     For the second part see that every tiling is characterised uniquely by the number of black tiles and their positions. Say there are  $d$  black tiles.Now we would characterise each black tiles by the first block it covers(since it is a  $1 \times 2$  tile). Now we will remove the  $2nd$  block from every black tile i.e we would a total of  $d$  of them and after our process we would append them next to the first block of the black tiles without altering the spacing between the remaining tiles that we are working with. Since the all black tiles are identical it won't affect our counting.
    But now our problem becomes much more simpler as now we have a total of  $n-d$  square blocks(remember those n removed blocks :)) and we have to choose  $d$  among them for being the  $1st$  block of the black tiles which we can do in  $\binom{n-d}{d}$  ways and now we are done with those black tiles and we are left with  $n-2d$  blocks which we can tile with any of the two different tiles remining i.e(blue,red) which can be done in  $2^{n-2d}$  ways. Now since these two tasks are dependent so we multiply them to get  $\binom{n-d}{d}2^{n-2d}$  for our particular  $d$ . Now summing this over all possible  $d's$  we get our required result.:)

Since  $x^{1/3}$  is increasing,
\[
\int_0^n x^{1/3} dx
\leq \sum_{k=1}^n k^{1/3}
\leq \int_1^{n+1} x^{1/3} dx.
\]
This implies that
\[
\sum_{k=1}^n k^{1/3}
= (\tfrac{3}{4}+o(1))n^{4/3},
\]
so the limit is only possible with  $(t,c)=(\frac{4}{3},\frac{3}{4})$ .

No need for heavy machinery. Let  $A = \dfrac{1}{n^{t - 4/3}}$  and  $\displaystyle{B = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac 1n \left(\frac{r}{n}\right)^{1/3}}$ . We know that \[\lim_{n \to \infty} B = \int_0^1 x^{1/3}dx = \frac 34\]
and we are given  $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to \infty} AB$  exists and is non zero, therefore \[\lim_{n\to \infty} A = \lim_{n\to \infty} \frac{AB}{B} = \dfrac{\lim_{n\to \infty} AB}{\lim_{n\to \infty} B}\]
also exists and is non zero which is only possible when  $t - \frac 43 = 0$  or  $t = \frac 43$  in which case  $c=\frac 34$ .

Say Rieman!
\begin{align*}
        c & = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \frac{1 + 2^{1/3} + 3^{1/3} + \dots + n^{1/3}}{n^t} \right)
        = & \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sqrt[3]{i}}{n^t} \right)
        = & \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sqrt[3]{\frac{i}{n}}}{n^{t-\frac{4}{3}}} \right)
        = & \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \frac{\int_{0}^{1} \sqrt[3]{x} dx}{n^{t-\frac{4}{3}}} \right)
        = & \lim_{n \to \infty} \left( \frac{\frac{3}{4}}{n^{t-\frac{4}{3}}} \right)
    \end{align*}
    If  $t=\frac{4}{3}$ ,  $c = \frac{3}{4}$ .
    If  $t>\frac{4}{3}$ ,  $c = \frac{\frac{3}{4}}{\infty} \to 0$     If  $t<\frac{4}{3}$ ,  $c = \frac{\frac{3}{4}}{\frac{1}{\infty}} \to \infty$     Hence, for  $c \in \mathbb{R} - \{0\}$ ,  $(c,t)= (\frac{3}{4}, \frac{4}{3})$ .
The essence of the above solutions is just to use   $\sum_n f(n) \sim \int f(x) dx$ . We can formalize this idea by using the squeeze theorem.

Suppose  $n\ge 2$ . Consider the polynomial \[Q_n(x) = 1-x^n - (1-x)^n .\]
Show that the equation  $Q_n(x) = 0$  has only two real roots, namely  $0$  and  $1$ .
solution_md:
$\bullet$   $\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Claim:}}$   $Q_{n}(x)$  has  no real zeros in  $(0,1)$ . $\bullet$   $\emph{Proof:}$  If  $\alpha \in(0,1)$  s.t.  $Q_n(\alpha)=0$  then  $\quad Q_n(0)=0, Q_n(\alpha)=0 \quad \text{and} \quad Q_n(\alpha)=0, Q_n(1)=0$ by Rolle's theorem  $\exists$   $c_1 \in(0, \alpha)$  s.t.  $Q_n^{\prime}\left(c_1\right)=0 \quad \& \quad c_2  \in (\alpha, 1)$  s.t.  $\quad Q_n^{\prime}\left(c_2\right)=0$  where  $c_2 \neq c_1$ .

Now,   $$ \begin{aligned}
& Q_n^{\prime}(x)=-n\left((1-x)^{n-1}-x^{n-1}\right) 
&  \implies Q_n^{\prime}(c_1)=-n\left(\left(1-c_1\right)^{n-1}-\left(c_1\right)^{n-1}\right)=0
\end{aligned} $$  only  $c_1=\frac{1}{2}$  is a real solution , Similarly  $c_2=\frac{1}{2} \quad$  but  $c_1 \neq c_2$ Hence not possible.  $\square$ Now If the real root of  $Q_{n}(x) \in \mathbb{R} \setminus [0,1]$  we divide the working as follows: $\bullet $   $\color{blue} \mathrm{Case 1:}$   $n$  is odd,

 Sps  $\exists$   $\quad \alpha \in \mathbb{R} \setminus [0,1]$  s.t.  $$ \begin{aligned}
Q_n(\alpha) & =0 \Rightarrow \quad 1-\alpha^n & =(1-\alpha)^n \Rightarrow \alpha^n-1=(\alpha-1)^n
\end{aligned} $$  for  $\alpha<0$  we have  $\alpha=-\alpha^{\prime} \quad\left(\alpha^{\prime}>0\right)$   $$ \begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow\left(\alpha^{\prime}\right)^n+1=\left(\alpha^{\prime}+1\right)^n 
& \Rightarrow \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\binom{n}{k}\left(\alpha^{\prime}\right)^{n-k}=0 \quad \text { but for } \alpha^{\prime}>0
\end{aligned} $$  this is not possible.  $(\star)$ for  $\alpha>1$  we notice  $$ \begin{aligned}
& Q_n(x)=Q_n(1-x) \Rightarrow Q_n(-(x-1))  =Q_n(x) 
& \Rightarrow \text { So } Q_n(-(\alpha-1))=Q_n(\alpha) \Rightarrow Q_n(-(\alpha-1))=0 
&
\end{aligned} $$  but  $-(\alpha-1)<0$  and at  $(\star)$  we just shown  $Q_n(x) \neq 0 \text { for } x<0$ Hence case of odd is not possible. $\bullet$   $\color{blue} \mathrm{Case 2:}$   $n$  is even

for  $\alpha>1 \quad Q_n(\alpha)<0$ for  $\alpha<0$  we have  $\alpha^n+(1-\alpha)^n=1$  replace  $\quad \alpha=-\alpha^{\star} \quad\left(\alpha^{\star}>0\right)$   $$ \left(\alpha^{\star}\right)^n+\left(1+\alpha^{\star}\right)^n=1 $$   which is not possible for  $\alpha^{\star}>0$  , hence we have exhausted all case , and hence only  $0,1$  are the only real roots of  $Q_{n}(x)$  for  $n \geqslant 2$ .  $\blacksquare$

*Solution:* We'll mainly use derivatives. Its straight-forward to verify that  $0$  and  $1$  are indeed always roots of  $Q_n(x)$ . Computing  $Q'_n(x)$  we get 
\[Q'_n(x) = n(1-x)^{n-1} - nx^{n-1}.\]
Its fairly easy to find that  $x = \frac{1}{2}$  is the only possible root of  $Q'_n(x)$ . By Fermat's Theorem, we know that the only possible local maxima/minima can occur only  $x = \frac{1}{2}$ . We now make two cases.

For the first case, consider  $n$  to be odd  $\iff n-1$  is even. Observe that under this case[don't worry about edge-cases like  $x = 0$  since it obviously works!]
\begin{align*}
Q'_n(x) \ge 0 &\iff (1-x)^{n-1} \ge x^{n-1} 
&\iff \left( \frac{1}{x} - 1\right)^{n-1} \ge 1 
&\iff \left| \frac{1}{x} - 1 \right| \ge 1 
&\iff x \in \left(-\infty, \frac{1}{2} \right] \coloneqq \mathcal{I}
\end{align*}
This means for odd  $n$ ,  $x = \frac{1}{2}$  is a local maxima since  $Q'_n(x) < 0$  for  $x \in \mathbb{R} - \mathcal{I}$  and  $Q'_n(x) \ge 0$  for  $x \in \mathcal{I}$ . This finishes the first case.
---------------------
Now, consider  $n$  to be even  $\iff n-1$  is odd. In this case, 
\[Q'_n(x) \ge 0 \iff (1-x)^{n-1} \ge x^{n-1}.\]
Here's the interesting part, all  $x \le 0$  work trivially! So, assume  $x > 0$ . This yields
\begin{align*}
Q'_n(x) \ge 0 &\iff \left( \frac{1}{x} - 1\right)^{n-1} \ge 1 
&\iff x \in \left(0, \frac{1}{2} \right]
\end{align*}
By a similar reasoning as above, we can again conclude  $x = \frac{1}{2}$  must be a point of local maxima again! Due to monotonic nature of  $Q_n(x)$ , it can have no more roots other than the ones already described. This concludes the solution.  $\blacksquare$

Assume   $$ Q_n(x) = 1 - x^n - (1 - x)^n $$  has  $\geq 3$  real roots. (Note that  $ Q_n(0) = Q_n(1) = 0 $ )

Then, by Rolle's theorem,  $$ Q_n'(x) = -n x^{n-1} + n(1 - x)^{n-1} $$  has  $\geq 2$  real roots.

But   $$ Q_n'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x^{n-1} = (1 - x)^{n-1} $$    $$ \Rightarrow |x| = |1 - x| $$    $$ \Rightarrow x \in \{1 - x, x - 1\} $$    $$ \Rightarrow x = 1 - x \Rightarrow x = \frac{1}{2} $$  which is a contradiction.

So  $ Q_n $  has two roots only, **null and unity**.  $\square$

Let  $P(x)$  be a polynomial with real coefficients. Let  $\alpha_1 , \dots , \alpha_k$  be the distinct real roots of  $P(x)=0$ . If  $P'$  is the derivative of  $P$ , show that for each  $i=1,\dots , k$  
\[\lim_{x\to \alpha_i} \frac{(x-\alpha_i)P'(x)}{P(x)} = r_i, \]
for some positive integer  $r_i$ .
solution_md:
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with real coefficients. Let $\alpha_1 , \dots , \alpha_k$ be the distinct real roots of $P(x)=0$ . If $P'$ is the derivative of $P$ , show that for each $i=1,\dots , k$ \[\lim_{x\to \alpha_i} \frac{(x-\alpha_i)P'(x)}{P(x)} = r_i, \] for some positive integer $r_i$ .
Cute!. ----- We can write $P(x)=(x-\alpha_1)^{r_1}(x-\alpha_2)^{r_2}(x-\alpha_3)^{r_3}\cdots (x-\alpha_{k})^{r_{k}}(x^2-a_{1}x+b_{1})^{t_1}(x^2-a_2x+b_2)^{t_{2}}\cdots (x^2-a_{\ell}x+b_{\ell})^{t_{\ell}}$ , where each of $x^2-a_{i}x+b_{i}$ have non real roots and real coefficients. Using logarithmic differentiation we have $\frac{P'(x)}{P(x)}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{r_{i}}{x-\alpha_{i}}+\sum_{j=1}^{\ell} \frac{t_{j} (2x-a_{j})}{x^2-a_{j}x+b_{j}}$ , so we have $\frac{(x-\alpha_{i})P'(x)}{P(x)}=\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{(x-\alpha_{i})r_{i}}{x-\alpha_{i}}+\sum_{j=1}^{\ell} \frac{(x-\alpha_{i})t_{j} (2x-a_{j})}{x^2-a_{j}x+b_{j}}$ , taking $\lim_{x\rightarrow \alpha_{i}} \frac{(x-\alpha_{i})P'(x)}{P(x)}$ we have the required limit to be $r_{i} \in \mathbb{Z}^{+}$ for each $i \in [k]$ . $\square$

It is useful to remember that the **logarithmic derivative** of a polynomial is given by the sum of  $\frac{m}{x-r}$  over all roots  $r$ , where  $m$  is the multiplicity of  $r$ .

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with real coefficients. Let $\alpha_1 , \dots , \alpha_k$ be the distinct real roots of $P(x)=0$ . If $P'$ is the derivative of $P$ , show that for each $i=1,\dots , k$ \[\lim_{x\to \alpha_i} \frac{(x-\alpha_i)P'(x)}{P(x)} = r_i, \] for some positive integer $r_i$ .
Let $r_i$ be the multiplicity of $\alpha _i$ as a root of $P$ . Hence we can write $$ P(x)=Q(x)\prod \limits _{i=1}^k(x-\alpha _i)^{r_i}, $$ where $Q$ is a polynomial without real roots. The key here is that\begin{align*}\frac{P'(x)}{P(x)} & =\frac{d}{dx}\log P(x) & =\frac{d}{dx}\log \left (Q(x)\prod \limits _{i=1}^k(x-\alpha _i)^{r_i}\right ) & =\frac{d}{dx}\left (\log Q(x)+\sum \limits _{i=1}^kr_i\log (x-\alpha _i)\right ) & =\frac{Q'(x)}{Q(x)}+\sum \limits _{i=1}^k\frac{r_i}{x-\alpha _i}. \end{align*}Hence $$ \frac{(x-\alpha _i)P'(x)}{P(x)}=\frac{(x-\alpha _i)Q'(x)}{Q(x)}+r_i+\sum \limits _{j=1,\,j\neq i}^nr_j\frac{x-\alpha _i}{x-\alpha _j}, $$ and therefore $$ \lim \limits _{x\to \alpha _i}\frac{(x-\alpha _i)P'(x)}{P(x)}=r_i, $$ which is a positive integer.

If $\alpha$ is a root of the polynomial $P(x)$ , then the multiplicity of $\alpha$ is the largest integer $r$ such that $(x - \alpha)^r$ divides $P(x)$ (which particularly implies that $(x - \alpha)^{r+1}$ does not divide it). Basically, it is the number of times $(x - \alpha)$ occurs in the factorisation of $P(x)$ .

stem_md: Let  $x_1 , \dots , x_{2024}$  be non negative real numbers with  $\displaystyle{\sum_{i=1}^{2024}}x_i = 1$ . Find, with proof, the minimum and maximum possible values of the following expression \[\sum_{i=1}^{1012} x_i + \sum_{i=1013}^{2024} x_i^2 .\]
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>I claim that the maximum is  $\boxed{1}$  and the minimum is  $\boxed{\frac{1}{1012}}.$ -----------------
Evidently,  $x_1, x_2,\dots, x_{2024} \in [0,1]$ . This suggests that  $x_i^2\leq x_i$ , where equality is attained only when  $x_i=0$  or  $x_i=1$ . 

Therefore,  $$ \sum_{i=1}^{1012} x_i + \sum_{i=1013}^{2024} x_i^2 \leq \sum_{i=1}^{2024}x_i = 1. $$  and it is easy to see that equality is indeed achieved when  $x_{1013}=x_{1014}=\dots = x_{2024}=0$  and  $\sum_{i=1}^{1012} x_i=1$ , or when  $x_k=1$  for some  $k\in\{1,2,\dots,2024\}$  and the rest is  $0$ . Hence, the maximum is  $1$ .  $\blacksquare$ ----------------
Now let  $\sum_{i=1}^{1012} x_i=\epsilon$  and  $\sum_{i=1013}^{2024} x_i = 1-\epsilon$ , where  $\epsilon\in[0,1]$ . By RMS-AM inequality, we get  $$ \sum_{i=1}^{1012} x_i + \sum_{i=1013}^{2024} x_i^2 \geq \sum_{i=1}^{1012} x_i + \frac{1}{1012}(\sum_{i=1013}^{2024} x_i)^2=\epsilon+\frac{(1-\epsilon)^2}{1012}, $$  which is minimized at  $\epsilon=0$ . Hence, the minimum turns out to be  $\frac{1}{1012}$ , which is achieved when  $x_1=x_2=\dots=x_{1012}=0$  and  $x_{1013}=x_{1014}=\dots=x_{2024}=\frac{1}{1012}$ , since the equality case of RMS-AM inequality is achieved when all the terms are equal.  $\blacksquare$</details>

But A is a sum of non-negative numbers  $A\ge 0$  , the function  $f(A)$  is increasing for  $A \ge 0$ , and its minimum occurs at  $A=0$ At  $A=0$ ,  $f(0)=\frac {1}{1012}$  $S=\sum_{i=1}^{1012}x_i+\sum_{i=1013}^{2024}x_i^2=1-\sum_{i=1013}^{2024}x_i+\sum_{i=1013}^{2024}x_i^2\ge 1-\sum_{i=1013}^{2024}x_i + \frac{\left(\sum_{i=1013}^{2024}x_i\right)^2}{1012}=f(A) \ge f(0)=\frac{1}{1012}$ Therefore  $S_{min}=\boxed{\frac{1}{1012}}$

stem_md:
In a sports tournament involving  $N$  teams, each team plays every other team exactly one. At the end of every match, the winning team gets  $1$  point and losing team gets  $0$  points. At the end of the tournament, the total points received by the individual teams are arranged in decreasing order as follows: \[x_1 \ge x_2 \ge \cdots 
\ge x_N . \]
Prove that for any  $1\le k \le N$ , \[\frac{N - k}{2} \le x_k \le N - \frac{k+1}{2}\]
solution_md:
Simple prob :) 
Let  $G_1=\{x_1,x_2,\cdots ,x_k\}$  and  $G_2=\{x_{k+1},\cdots ,x_N\}$ .
Then  $$ kx_k\leq \sum_{i=1}^{k}x_i\leq \underset{\text{G1 vs G1}}{k\choose{2}} +\underset{\text{G1 vs G2}}{k(n-k)} $$    $$ \Longrightarrow  x_k \leq N - \frac{k+1}{2} $$  Also let Let  $G_3=\{x_1,x_2,\cdots ,x_{k-1}\}$  and  $G_4=\{x_k,\cdots ,x_N\}$ .
Then  $$ (N-k+1)x_k\geq \sum_{i=k}^{n}x_i\geq \underset{\text{G4 vs G4}}{N-k-1\choose{2}} +\underset{\text{G4 vs G3}}{0} $$    $$ \Longrightarrow  x_k \geq \frac{N-k}{2} $$  Therefore   $$ \frac{N - k}{2} \le x_k \le N - \frac{k+1}{2} $$  as desired.

stem_md:
Let  $f: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$  be a function which is differentiable at  $0$ . Define another function  $g: \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$  as follows:   $$ g(x) = \begin{cases}
f(x)\sin\left(\frac 1x\right) ~ &\text{if} ~ x \neq 0 

0 &\text{if} ~ x = 0.
 \end{cases} $$  Suppose that  $g$  is also differentiable at  $0$ . Prove that \[g'(0) = f'(0) = f(0) = g(0) = 0.\]
solution_md: The solutions in the thread are way too complicated. Let me simplify it for you people! ;) *Solution:* We will mainly rely on the following high-school textbook lemmas which we will state without proofs since they're standard.**Lemma:** For any functions $p,q$ with $\lim_{x \to a} p(x) = L_1$ and $\lim_{x \to a} q(x) = L_2 \ne 0$ , then $\lim_{x \to a} \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}$ exists and is precisely $L_1/L_2$ .**Lemma:** If a function $h(x)$ is differentiable at $c$ then it must be continuous at $c$ as well. We're all set for the solution.**Claim:** $f(0) = 0$ . *Proof:* Observe since $g$ is differentiable at $0$ , then it must continuous at $0$ as well. Same goes for $f$ . So we have \begin{align*} \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = 0 \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = f(0) \end{align*} If $f(0) \ne 0$ , then dividing the above equations will yield that $\lim_{x \to 0} \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)$ exists and is $0$ which is a contradiction. This means $f(0) = 0$ as desired. $\square$ --------- Using differentiability of $g$ and $f$ we get that \begin{align*} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x) \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) - 0}{x-0} \coloneqq c_1 \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x-0} \coloneqq c_2 \end{align*} If $f'(0) \ne 0$ , then dividing above two limits yield a similar contradiction as the previous case. Therefore, we can also say that $f'(0) = 0$ and $c_2 = 0$ . Here's the final part... Observe that \[-\frac{f(x)}{x} \le \frac{f(x) \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)}{x} \le \frac{f(x)}{x}\] Then by the *Squeeze Theorem* in conjunction with limit definition of $f'(0)$ , we can finally conclude that $g'(0) = 0$ . The solution is now complete. $\blacksquare$

Consider a container of the shape obtained by revolving a segment of parabola  $x = 1 + y^2$  around the  $y$ -axis as shown below. The container is initially empty. Water is poured at a constant rate of  $1\, \text{cm}^3$  into the container. Let  $h(t)$  be the height of water inside container at time  $t$ . Find the time  $t$  when the rate of change of  $h(t)$  is maximum.

**Attachments:**

![2024_P7.jpeg](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/0/4/e5652dbc5ddebd4210f254384db00d71654d6b.jpeg)
solution_md:
Okay... Same as above, but I will still post I think.

*Solution:* Rotate the diagram and consider the function  $f(x) = 1 + x^2$ . We now need to compute the volume from  $x = -1$  to  $x = h(t)$  obtained by revolving  $f$  around  $x$ -axis. By a well-known formula, we know that the volume  $V$  is precisely 
\[ V(t) = \int_{-1}^{h(t)} \pi (1+x^2)^2 \, dx .\]
Differentiate with respect to  $t$  using the *Chain Rule* and the *Leibiniz Rule* keeping in mind that  $\frac{dV}{dt} = 1$ . This yields that
\[1 = \pi\left(1+h(t))^2\right)^2 \frac{dh}{dt}.\]
It is easy to see that  $dh/dt$  is maximized when  $h(t)$  is  $0$ . This means maximum is attained at  $h(t) = 0$ . If we let  $t'$  be the instant when  $h(t) = 0$ [ $h$  is obviously an increasing function(thus injective) due to physical constraints] then 
\[V(t') = \pi \int_{-1}^{0} (1+x^2)^2 \, dx = \frac{28}{15}\pi \, \text{unit}^3.\]
Finally, since rate of change of volume is constant and precisely  $1$ [just for the sake of proof why unitary method works, just solve the simple linear differential equation  $dV/dt = 1$  with constraint  $V(0) = 0$ ], we can find out that  $V(t') = \frac{28}{15}\pi \iff t' = \frac{28}{15}\pi$  with suitable of choice of unit of time.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $a,b,c$  be nonzero real numbers such that  $a+b+c \neq 0$ . Assume that   $$ \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} + \frac{1}{c} = \frac{1}{a+b+c} $$   Show that for any odd integer  $k$ ,   $$ \frac{1}{a^k} + \frac{1}{b^k} + \frac{1}{c^k} = \frac{1}{a^k+b^k+c^k}. $$
solution_md:
This is probably a problem which you'd see in some basic IOQM/PRMO/AMC/AIME type training. I honestly did not do my training properly, I would have missed this factorization which people have posted here :( I'd not say that this problem is really bad or anything because other problems were at a fairly good level. My personal preference is a balanced paper, but maybe this works as well. Nevertheless, we will not miss our chance to learn the technique of homogenization ;)

*Solution:* Clearing out denominator, we get the following equation.
\[ (ab+bc+ca)(a + b + c) = abc\]
Both sides of the equation are clearly homogenous with degree  $3$ . Therefore, we can assume without loss of generality, that  $a + b + c = 1$ . This gives 
\[abc - ab - bc -ca = 0.\]
Here's the clever observation, 
\begin{align*}
(a-1)(b-1)(c-1) &= abc - ab - bc - ca + a + b + c -1 
&= 0
\end{align*}
Therefore one of  $a,b,c$  must be  $1$ . Assume  $b = 1$ , then putting this back into  $a+b+c=1$  yields  $a = -c$ . Finally, 
\[ \frac{1}{a^k} + \frac{1}{b^k} + \frac{1}{c^k} = 1 = \frac{1}{a^k+b^k+c^k}\] 
where of course we have used the fact that  $(-a)^k = -a^k$  where  $k$  is an odd natural.  $\blacksquare$ <details><summary>Clarification</summary>If the reader is not comfortable with the "WLOG  $a+b+c = 1$ ", then here's a quick proof why it works. Think of fixing the sum  $a+b+c = M$ . Now you want to prove the big equation at the end with a constraint  $a+b+c = M$ . This obviously doesn't prove it for entire non-zero reals, but you do you manage to prove it for a subset. Now, what if you set  $M$  free? This means  $M$  could have been  $1,2,3,\sqrt{\pi}$  anything. Basically say  $M = 4040$ , and you manage to prove the big equation. You must have used a series of steps to show it under " $4040$  assumption". The magic is, you could use the same series of step for any real number  $M$ !

So, set  $a = a'M$ ,  $b = b'M$  and  $c = c'M$ . This would yield  $a' + b' + c' = 1$ . If you put this back into the equation  $(ab+bc+ca)(a + b + c) = abc$ , then you will get the equation  $a'b' + b'c' + c'a' = a'b'c'$ . This is the same equation! It is just that you've  $a+b+c = 1$ . That's the magic of homogenization/normalization!</details>

stem_md: If the interior angles of a triangle  $ABC$  satisfy the equality,   $$ \sin ^2 A + \sin ^2 B + \sin^2  C = 2 \left( \cos ^2 A + \cos ^2 B + \cos ^2 C \right), $$   prove that the triangle must have a right angle.
solution_md:
$\sin ^2 A + \sin ^2 B + \sin^2 C = 2 \left( \cos ^2 A + \cos ^2 B + \cos ^2 C \right) \Longrightarrow \cos ^2 A + \cos ^2 B + \cos ^2 C + \sin ^2 A + \sin ^2 B + \sin^2 C = 3 \left( \cos ^2 A + \cos ^2 B + \cos ^2 C \right) \Longrightarrow \cos ^2 A + \cos ^2 B + \cos ^2 C = 1$ .
Now,  $\cos ^2 A + \cos ^2 B  = \sin^2 C = \sin^2 (A+B) = \sin^2 A \cos^2 B + \cos^2 A + \sin^2 B + 2 \sin A \sin B \cos A \cos B$ .
So,  $\cos^2 A \left( 1 - \sin ^2 B \right) + \cos ^2 B \left( 1 - \sin ^2 A \right) = 2 \sin A \sin B \cos A \cos B$ .
So,  $2 \cos ^2 A \cos ^2 B = 2 \sin A \sin B \cos A \cos B$ .
So,  $\cos A \cos B \cos(A+B) = 0 = \cos A \cos B \cos C$ .
Since  $A,B,C \in \left( 0 , \pi \right)$ , atleast one of  $A,B,C$  must equal  $\frac{\pi}{2}$ .  $\square$

Okay, I'm slow at trigonometry... A 20 minutes solve, although very very sad to hear its a ISI B.Math PYQ. *Solution:* We will prove one claim which will finish the problem on the spot. The main idea is to get rid of the square terms and simplify it down to angles of the triangle.**Claim:** For angles of triangle $A,B$ and $C$ we have \[\cos(2A) + \cos(2B) + \cos(2C) = 4\cos(A)\cos(B)\cos(C) - 1.\] *Proof:* We will use sum to product formulae and use the fact that $A+B+C = \pi$ to prove this. \begin{align*} \cos(2A) + \cos(2B) + \cos(2C) &= 2\cos(A+B)\cos(A-B) + 2\cos^2(C)-1 &= 2\cos(\pi - C)\cos(\pi-C-2B) + 2\cos(C)-1 &= 2\cos(C)\left(\cos(2B+C) +\cos(C) \right) - 1 &= 2\cos(C)2\cdot\cos(B+C)\cos(B) - 1 &= 4\cos(A)\cos(B)\cos(C)-1. \end{align*} This proves the claim. $\square$ ---------------------- Adding $2(\sin^2(A)+\sin^2(B)+\sin^2(C))$ to the original equation we get \[ 3 \sum \sin^2(A) = 6 \implies \sum \sin^2(A) = 2.\] Using the half angle formula of $\frac{1-\cos(2A)}{2} = \sin^2(A)$ , we get \[ \sum \frac{1-\cos(2A)}{2} = 2 \implies \sum \cos(2A) = -1.\] Finally, on applying the proved claim, we get that \[4\cos(A)\cos(B)\cos(C) = 0\] which forces one of $A,B,C$ to be $\pi/2$ , finishing the solution. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $\mathbb{N}$  denote the set of natural numbers, and let  $\left( a_i, b_i \right)$ ,  $1 \leq i \leq 9$ , be nine distinct tuples in  $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ . Show that there are three distinct elements in the set  $\{ 2^{a_i} 3^{b_i} \colon 1 \leq i \leq 9 \}$  whose product is a perfect cube.
solution_md:
This one is easy. Let  $S =\{ 2^{a_i} 3^{b_i} \colon 1 \leq i \leq 9 \}$ . So cardinality of  $S$  is  $9$ . Consider another set  $A$  of pair of powers  $(a,b)$  in  $mod3$ . This gives a total of  $9$  possibilities.  $\{(0,0),(0,1),(0,2),(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)\}$ . If any pair appears for atleast three times or if all pairs appear for exactly one time, we are done. We need to check for the rest case. For this, make three subsets of set  $A$  and define   $A'=\{(0,0),(0,1),(0,2)\}$ ,  $A''=\{(1,0),(1,1),(1,2)\}$ ,  $A'''=\{(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)\}$ . Notice that if three pairs of powers belongs to either of these subsets, their product will be a perfect cube. If we choose exactly two pairs from each set then we have to choose one more pair so either we have  $A'$ , or  $A''$ , or  $A'''$ . This completes the proof.

stem_md: Let  $n \geq 2$  and let  $a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots \leq a_n$  be positive integers such that  $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i = \prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i$ . Prove that  $\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \leq 2n$  and determine when equality holds.
solution_md: Done with the help of the hints from some of my seniors and **MathematicalArceus**. -------------------------- Claim: For any positive integers $m_1, m_2, \cdots, m_n$ , $(m_1 + 1)(m_2+1) \cdots (m_n + 1) \geq 2( m_1 + m_2 + \cdots + m_n)$ . *Proof.* We proceed using induction. The base case is trivial. Assume that for any given $k$ integer this works. We will prove that if we add arbitrary integer to it, it still holds true. $(m_1 + 1) \cdots (m_n + 1)(m_{n+1} + 1) \geq 2(m_1 + m_2 + \cdots + m_n)(m_{n+1} + 1) \geq 2(m_1 + m_2 + \cdots m_n) + 2m_1m_{n+1} \geq 2(m_1 + m_2 + \cdots m_{n+1}$ . $\square$ --------------------------- Let there be $k$ many $1$ 's. So, $\forall i >k$ , $a_i >1$ . So, $a_1a_2 \cdots a_n = a_{k+1}a_{k+2} \cdots a_n \geq 2(a_{k+1} \cdots a_n - (n-k)) \geq 2(a_{k+1} \cdots a_n - n) = 2a_1a_2 \cdots a_n - 2n$ . So, $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \leq 2n$ . $\square$ -------------------------- Equality holds iff $(a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_{n-1}, a_n) = (1,1, \cdots, 1, 2, n)$ . $\square$

Write
\[
r=\#\{\,i:a_i=1\},
\qquad
k=n-r,
\]
and label the remaining entries \(b_1,\dots,b_k\), so \(b_j\ge2\) for each \(j\).  Then
\[
\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}
=\{\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_r,b_1,\dots,b_k\},
\qquad
r+k=n.
\]
Consider the monic polynomial
\[
f(x)\;=\;\prod_{i=1}^n (x-a_i)
\;=\;(x-1)^r\prod_{j=1}^k (x-b_j).
\]
By Viète’s formulas its first and last elementary‐symmetric sums are
\[
\sigma_1
=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i
=r + \sum_{j=1}^k b_j,
\qquad
\sigma_n
=\prod_{i=1}^n a_i
=\prod_{j=1}^k b_j.
\]
The hypothesis \(\sigma_1=\sigma_n\) becomes
\[
r \;+\;\sum_{j=1}^k b_j
\;=\;\prod_{j=1}^k b_j.
\]
Set
\[
S=\sum_{j=1}^k b_j,
\quad
P=\prod_{j=1}^k b_j.
\]
Then \(r=P-S\), and
\[
n=r+k = (P-S)+k,
\quad
\sum_{i=1}^n a_i = \sigma_1 = P.
\]
Hence
\[
2n \;=\;2\bigl(P-S+k\bigr)
\;=\;2P \;-\;2S \;+\;2k,
\]
so the inequality \(\sum a_i\le2n\) is equivalent to
\[
P \;\le\;2P \;-\;2S \;+\;2k
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
P \;-\;2S \;+\;2k\;\ge0.
\]
But since each \(b_j\ge2\) we have
\[
S\;=\;\sum_{j=1}^k b_j\;\ge\;2k,
\qquad
P\;=\;\prod_{j=1}^k b_j\;\ge\;2^k.
\]
Therefore
\[
P - 2S +2k
\;\ge\;
2^k \;-\;2\,(2k)\;+\;2k
\;=\;
2^k -2k
\;\ge\;0
\]
because \(2^k\ge2k\) for all \(k\ge1\).  This proves
\(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=P\le2n\).


Equality in the chain
\[
2^k\;\ge\;2k
\]
holds exactly when \(k=1\) or \(k=2\).  But
- If \(k=1\), then \(P=b_1=2^1=2\) and \(S=b_1=2\), so \(r=P-S=0\) and \(n=r+1=1\), contradicting \(n\ge2\).  
- If \(k=2\), then \(P=b_1b_2=2^2=4\) and \(S=b_1+b_2=2k=4\), so
  \[
    b_1+b_2=4,
    \quad
    b_1b_2=4
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    \{b_1,b_2\}=\{2,2\}.
  \]
  Hence \(r=P-S=4-4=0\) and \(n=r+2=2\), giving \(\{a_1,a_2\}=\{2,2\}\).

These two cases together force the only way to achieve \(\sum a_i=2n\) under the original
\(\sum a_i=\prod a_i\) hypothesis is, up to order,
\[
\{a_1,\dots,a_n\}
=\{\underbrace{1,\dots,1}_{n-2\text{ times}},\,2,\,n\}.
\]
Indeed for that multiset one checks
\(\sum a_i=(n-2)+2+n=2n\) and \(\prod a_i=1^{n-2}\cdot2\cdot n=2n\).

Let  $S^1 = \{ z \in \mathbb{C} \mid |z| =1 \}$  be the unit circle in the complex plane. Let  $f \colon S^1 \longrightarrow S^2$  be the map given by  $f(z) = z^2$ . We define  $f^{(1)} \colon = f$  and  $f^{(k+1)} \colon = f \circ f^{(k)}$  for  $k \geq 1$ . The smallest positive integer  $n$  such that  $f^{(n)}(z) = z$  is called the *period* of  $z$ . Determine the total number of points in  $S^1$  of period  $2025$ .
(Hint :  $2025 = 3^4 \times 5^2$ )
solution_md: Incomplete SolutionThis is an incomplete solution. -------------------------- Claim: $f^{(k)}(z) = z^{2^{k}}$ . *Proof.* We proceed using induction. Base case is trivial. Assume that it works for $k = n$ . $f^{(n+1)} = f \circ f^{(n)} = f\left(z^{2^{n}} \right) = z^{2^{n} \cdot 2} = z^{2^{n+1}}$ . ------------------------- Now, $f^{2025}(z) = z^{2^{2025}}$ . All numbers who have a *period* of $2025$ are a subset of all the roots of the equation $z^{2^{2025}} = z$ . Since $z \neq 0$ , they are the subset of the roots of $z^{2^{2025}-1} = 1$ . The set of the roots of the equation $R = \{ \cos \frac{2k \pi}{2^{2025} -1} + i \sin \frac{2k \pi}{2^{2025} -1} \mid k \in \{0,1,2,3, \cdots, 2^{2025} -2 \} \}$ . Any number $t$ that divides $2^{2025} -1$ , $\cos \frac{2t \pi}{2^{2025} -1} + i \sin \frac{2t \pi}{2^{2025} -1}$ cannot have a *period* of $2025$ since they have a period less than that. Hence the number of numbers that have a period of $2025$ are $\boxed{\phi \left( 2^{2025} -1 \right)}$ . $\square$

<details><summary>Here is a concrete solution.</summary>For every  $z$  such that  $|z|=1$  and  $z^{2^n -1} = 1$ , there exists a smallest positive integer  $d$  such that  $z^{2^d -1}=1$ . We can show that for this to hold,  $n$  must be divisible by  $d$ . To prove this, first show that  $z^{2^n -1}=1$  and  $z^{2^d -1}=1$  implies  $z^{\gcd(2^n -1, 2^d -1)} = 1$ . This follows by a standard proof technique where you run Euclidean algorithm of finding g.c.d. in the exponent. The same technique also gives you  $\gcd(2^n -1, 2^d -1)=2^{\gcd(n, d)}-1$ . The upshot of this is that if  $d$  does not divide  $n$ , then  $\gcd(d,n)<d$  which combined with  $z^{2^{\gcd(n,d)}-1}=1$  contradicts the minimality of  $d$ .

Next, denote by  $A_d$  the set of  $z$  on  $|z|=1$  such that  $z^{2^d -1}=1$  the first time for  $d$ , that is,  $z^{2^k -1}\neq 1$  for any  $k<d$ . By definition, these sets  $A_d$  are disjoint. Using what we showed above, taking union of these sets for all divisors  $d$  of n gives the set of  $z$  such that  $|z|=1$  and  $z^{2^n -1} = 1$ . We can therefore write   $$ \sum_{d\mid n} |A_d| = 2^n -1. $$  Next step is to use the above equation recursively, first for powers of a prime. For convenience, write  $a_d=|A_d|$ . 
For  $n=p^m$ , note that  $2^{p^m} - 1 = \sum_{d \mid p^m} a_d = \sum_{d \mid p^{m-1}} a_d + a_{p^m} = 2^{p^{m-1}}-1 + a_{p^m}$ , which gives   $$ a_{p^m} = 2^{p^m} - 2^{p^{m-1}}. $$   
Next, you can apply similar principle to find  $a_{p^m q^r}$  for distinct primes  $p$  and  $q$ . This suffices for  $2025=3^4\times 5^2$ . I am leaving the remaining computation.</details> edit: just found its mostly similar to a solution by some juniors of mine, so credit goes to them!

For the rest of the solutions, we define that  $a_n = 2^n- 1$ . Now, note that  $z$  has period  $k$  if  $z$  is a  $(2^k-1)$  th root of unity but for any  $i <k$ ,  $i$  is not the period so ,  $ z$  is not a  $a_i$  th root of unity. We define that  $ n$  is a "general period" of  $z$  if  $z^{a_n} = 1$  and  $n$  is said to be a "non-fundamental period" if  $n$  is a general period of  $z$  but  $\exists\,\, j<n$  such that  $j$  is the period of  $z$  or equivalently,  $z^{a_j} = 1$ . 

 If  $z$  has period  $2025$  then  $z$  is a  $2^{2025}-1$  th root of unity.
Now number of such  $z \in S^1$  such that  $ 2025$  is a general period of  $z $  is  $ a_{2025 }$ . Let this set be denoted by  $P_{2025}$ We want to find and exclude the number of  $ z \in P_{2025}$  such that  $ 2025$  is a non-fundamental period.
Say,  $z$  be such a complex number with  $k<2025$  is the period of  $z$ , so,  $z^{a_k} = 1 \,\, , z^{a_{2025}} = 1$ . So,  $a_k \vert a_{2025} \implies k \vert 2025$ . Now if  $k$  divides  $2025$  but is smaller than  $2025$  then power of  $3$  or power of  $5$  is at least one less than that of in  $2025$ .
So,  $ k \vert 675$  or  $k\vert 405$ . So,  $675$  or  $405$  has to be a general period of  $ z$ .  


Number of such  $z$  for which  $675$  is a general period  $ = a_{675}$ Number of such  $z$  for which  $405$   is a general  period  $ = a_{405}$ Number of such  $z$  for which both  $675$  and  $405$  are general period  =  $ a_{135}$  ( They will have general period  $3^3\cdot 5$ )
So number of  $z$  on  $S^1$  with period  $ 2025  =  a_{2025}-a_{675}-a_{405}+a_{135} = 2^{2025}-2^{675}-2^{405}+2^{135}$

Replace  $2025$  by  $n$ . Essentially, what we want is the number of complex values  $z$  such that  $z^{2^n-1}=1$  but  $z^{2^d-1}\neq 1$  for all  $d\mid n$  with  $d<n$ . 

Suppose  $n=p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}\dots p_k^{\alpha_k}$ , where  $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$  are primes.

The answer is   $$ \boxed{2^n-1-\sum_{j=1}^k (-1)^{j+1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i_1< i_2< \cdots <i_j\leq k} 2^{\frac{n}{p_{i_1}p_{i_2}\dots p_{i_j}}}-1\right)}. $$   
This expression is routinely derived from PIE. We exclude the roots of  $z^{2^{\frac{n}{p_1}}-1}=1$ , the roots of  $z^{2^{\frac{n}{p_2}}-1}=1$ , and so on, from the roots of  $z^{2^n-1}=1$ . But during this process, we removed the roots of  $z^{2^{\frac{n}{p_ip_j}}-1}=1$ , where  $1\leq i<j\leq k$ , in excess, so we must add them back. And now, we added the roots of  $z^{2^{\frac{n}{p_ip_jp_l}}-1}=1$ , where  $1\leq i<j<l\leq k$  in excess, so we have to remove them from our counting. Thus, we continue this inclusion–exclusion process to get the expression mentioned above.  

In particular, for  $n=2025=3^4\cdot 5^2$ , this comes out to be   $$ 2^{2025}-1-(2^{675}-1+2^{405}-1)+2^{135}-1=\boxed{2^{2025}-2^{675}-2^{405}+2^{135}}. $$   
<details><summary>Remark</summary>Note that  $\phi\left (2^{2025} -1\right)$  undercounts, because it counts the number of complex roots of  $z^{2^{2025}-1}=1$  for which  $z^d\neq 1$ , where  $d\mid 2^{2025}-1$ . Whereas what we actually want is the number of complex roots of  $z^{2^{2025}-1}=1$  for which  $z^{2^d-1}\neq 1$ , where  $d\mid 2025$ . Indeed, there are several factors of  $2^{2025} -1$  which are not of the form  $2^d-1$  with  $d\mid 2025$ . For example, one is  $151$ .  :)</details>
<details><summary>Further generalization</summary>Replace  $f(z)=z^2$  by  $f(z)=z^r$ , where  $r\in\mathbb{Q}$ . Suppose  $r=\frac{x}{y}$  where  $x, y\in\mathbb{Z}$  and  $\gcd(x, y)=1$ . We want the roots of  $$ z^{\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^n}=z\implies z^{\left|\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^n-1\right|}=1\implies z^{\left|x^n-y^n\right|}=1 $$  for which  $z^{\left|x^d-y^d\right|}\neq 1$  for all  $d\mid n$  with  $d<n$ . Suppose  $n=p_1^{\alpha_1}p_2^{\alpha_2}\dots p_k^{\alpha_k}$ , where  $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$  are primes. Again, we apply PIE to get the answer:  $$ \boxed{\left|x^n-y^n\right|-\sum_{j=1}^k (-1)^{j+1}\left(\sum_{1\leq i_1< i_2< \cdots <i_j\leq k} \left|x^{\frac{n}{p_{i_1}p_{i_2}\dots p_{i_j}}}-y^{\frac{n}{p_{i_1}p_{i_2}\dots p_{i_j}}}\right|\right)}. $$</details>

Solution motivated by the Möbius inversion formula. 

Let 
\[
S^1 = \{z\in\mathbb{C}\mid |z|=1\},
\]
and define  $f\colon S^1\to S^1$  by  $f(z)=z^2$ .  By induction one shows
\[
f^{(n)}(z)=z^{2^n},\quad n\ge1.
\]
Thus
\[
f^{(n)}(z)=z
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
z^{2^n-1}=1.
\]
Let
\[
S_n = \bigl\{z\in S^1 : f^{(n)}(z)=z\bigr\}
= \bigl\{z\in S^1 : z^{2^n-1}=1\bigr\}.
\]
Since the equation  $z^{2^n-1}=1$  has exactly  $2^n-1$  distinct solutions on  $S^1$ , we have
\[
\lvert S_n\rvert = 2^n - 1.
\]

Denote by  $P(n)$  the number of points of *exact* period  $n$ .  Then every  $z\in S_n$  has period  $d$  for some  $d\mid n$ , and these are disjoint.  Hence
\[
S_n \;=\;\bigsqcup_{d\mid n} P(d),
\]
and by Möbius inversion,
\[
P(n)
=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\,\bigl\lvert S_{\,n/d}\bigr\rvert
=\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)\Bigl(2^{\,\frac n d}-1\Bigr).
\]

Now take  $n=2025=3^4\cdot5^2$ .  Its square‐free divisors are  $d=1,3,5,15$ , with
\[
\mu(1)=1,\quad \mu(3)=-1,\quad\mu(5)=-1,\quad\mu(15)=1,
\]
and
\[
\frac{2025}{1}=2025,\quad
\frac{2025}{3}=675,\quad
\frac{2025}{5}=405,\quad
\frac{2025}{15}=135.
\]
Hence
\begin{align*}
P(2025)
&=\;(2^{2025}-1)\;-\;(2^{675}-1)\;-\;(2^{405}-1)\;+\;(2^{135}-1)
&=2^{2025}-2^{675}-2^{405}+2^{135}.
\end{align*}
Therefore, the total number of points in  $S^1$  of period  $2025$  is
\[
\boxed{2^{2025}-2^{675}-2^{405}+2^{135}}.
\]

Sure, olympiad people will call it trivial, but someone who hasn't been trained well enough in olympiad geometry, this isn't an easy problem by any means. Finding a construction is not trivial at all. Even if you start angle chasing, to find something, claiming that  $A-I-D$  is collinear is not at all easy! So, for the newcomers, don't worry its not that easy. You've now a lesson to learn all the basic olympiad geometry configurations, like the orthic triangle and some incenter configurations. It's not that difficult, you guys can do it. I think the problem quality was okay, but I agree its quite disappointing for the people who already knew the configuration and a very easy solve rate. The problem is pretty nice, but the fact that this well-known to some students just makes kinda undesirable on the test.

Here's a solution which proves uniqueness. I'll also show that the answer is unique given that its an acute triangle.

*Solution:* We will prove that such a path must necessarily form the orthic triangle of  $\triangle ABC$ . 

First we will assume that  $\triangle DEF$  is indeed the orthic triangle and show it works. Let  $H$  be the orthocenter of  $\triangle ABC$ , then  $\odot(HDBF), \odot(HFAE)$  and  $\odot(HECD)$  must be cyclic with diameters  $HB, HA$  and  $HC$  respectively. Then finally 
\[\angle HDF= \angle HBF = \angle EBF = \angle FCA = \angle HCE = \angle HDE\] 
which shows that  $H$  bisects angle  $FDE$ . Since  $HD \perp BC$ , by symmetry we can conclude that his path works.

For the other direction, let  $I$  be the incenter of  $\triangle DEF$ . Then its clear that perpendiculars on  $BC, CA, AB$  from  $D,E$  and  $F$  respectively concur at  $I$ . From here it is sufficient to show that  $A-I-D$  are collinear. Let 


- $\angle FDI = \angle IDE = x$ ;
- $\angle DEI = \angle IEF = y$ ;
- $\angle EFI = \angle IFD = z$ .

From angle sum property in  $\triangle DEF$ , we also get that  $x + y + z = 90^\circ$ . It's obvious that  $\odot(AFEI)$  is cyclic with diameter  $\overline{AI}$ . Finally
\begin{align*}
\angle AID &= \angle AIF + \angle FID 
&= \angle AEF + (180^\circ - x - y) 
&= (90^\circ - z)+ (180^\circ - x - y) = 180^\circ.
\end{align*}
which completes the proof.  $\blacksquare$

Suppose an esteemed gentleman is attempting to solve this problem and absolutely DESTROY this question, through an improvisatory method. The process has some stages, so let me explain it to everyone. Consider a robot that travels in a loop. The bot's mechanism is like this: the system operates on an acute triangle, and to run the robot I have to just consider a point and some line through the point. Note the point chosen must be chosen within the triangle or else the bot will fail to run. Once done, the robot will move along the line made until it hits one side of the triangle, at which point it reflects off the side of the triangle following the law of reflection. This repeats on and on. If the bot hits a side at a different point to where it hit the first time, it self-destructs, certainly an undesirable outcome. So how can we choose a point and line so the bot works indefinitely?
Now this problem is very interesting, because it relies on the fundamental properties of the orthic triangle. Notably, the orthic triangle forms angle bisectors using the original altitudes. Furthermore, the original triangle *has* to be acute or else the orthic triangle does not lie fully within the original triangle, resulting in the bot self-destructing.

Hence  $a_n\rightarrow a\in R$ . Then  $a_{n+1}=f(a_n)\rightarrow f(a)$  and  $f(a)=a$ .

This problem can be found in Art-n-Craft book by Paul Zeitz, but with a more general case where $\frac 1 2$ is replaced any constant $k < 1$ and $f'(x) {\color{red} \le} k$ . In the exercises, it is even discussed why $k < 1$ is chosen and why would we not write $f'(x) < 1$ directly. It's a really good problem and everyone should look for it. I'll present the same solution as in the book and I acknowledge this solution isn't mine. Although, honestly speaking, Banach FIxed Point Theorem was the first thing which striked my mind, but even this works wonderfully!
Suppose $f$ is differentiable on $(-\infty, \infty)$ and there is a constant $k < 1$ such that $f'(x) \le k$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ . Show that $f$ must have a fixed point.
*Solution:* Consider the intuitive auxillary function $g(x) \coloneqq f(x) - x$ . If there are two points $a,b$ such that $g(a)g(b) < 0$ , then by the *Intermediate Value Theorem* one can conclude that $g$ must have a root, which would finish on the spot. Therefore we would assume that $g$ is either strictly positive, or strictly negative. For our solution, WLOG assume that $g > 0$ . Apply *Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem* on $[0,x]$ on the function $f$ (take $x > 0$ ). This yields that there exists some constant $c \in (0,x)$ such that \[ \frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x} = f'(c)\] Since $g > 0$ , we must have $f(x) > x$ . This yields \[k \ge f'(c) > 1 - \frac{f(0)}{x}. \] Taking $x$ large enough, we would get that $1-\frac{f(0)}{x} > k$ which would be a contradiction. Therefore $g$ can't be positive everytime, which show that $g$ must have a root, as desired. The other case is omitted from the book. For the other case, basically do the same argument from left side. This time we will assume $f(x) < x$ for all $x$ apply MVT on the interval $[-x,0]$ where $x > 0$ again. This time you should get \[ -k \le -f'(c) < -1 - \frac{f(0)}{x}\] multiplying everything by $-1$ and taking large $x$ suffices. $\blacksquare$

Define

By the Extreme Value Theorem,  $f(x)$  attains a maximum and minimum on  $[0,1]$ .

Let
\[
M = \max_{x \in [0,1]} f(x), \quad \text{and suppose } M = f(k) \text{ for some } k \in [0,1].
\]

We are given that  $f(x)$  has an extremum at  $x=0$ . Assume, for contradiction, that this is not the global maximum. Then there exists  $k \in (0,1]$  such that  $f(k) \geq f(0)$ .

By the Lagrange Mean Value Theorem on  $[0,k]$ , there exists  $c_k \in (0,k)$  such that
\[
\frac{f(k) - f(0)}{k} = f'(c_k).
\]

\[
\frac{f(k)}{k} = f'(c_k).
\]
Thus,
\[
f(k) = k f'(c_k).
\]
From the given condition  $|f'(x)| \leq f(x)$ , we get:
\[
f'(c_k) \leq f(c_k) \Rightarrow k f'(c_k) \leq k f(c_k).
\]
Hence,
\[
f(k) \leq k f(c_k).
\]

Since  $k \in (0,1)$ , this implies  $f(k) < f(c_k)$ , contradicting the maximality of  $f(k)$ . Therefore, the maximum must occur at  $x = 0$ .

Thus,  $f$  achieves its maximum and minimum at  $x = 0$ , and has an extremum there. Therefore,  $f$  must be constant on  $[0,1]$ .

Hence,
\[
f(x) \equiv f(0).
\]

From the condition  $f'(x) \leq f(x)$  and the fact that  $f$  is constant, we have  $f'(x) = 0$ , so:
\[
0 \leq f(x) \leq 0 \Rightarrow f(x) = 0.
\]

\[
\boxed{f(x) \equiv 0 \text{ on } [0,1]} \quad \blacksquare
\]

Let \( t \in (0,1) \) be a real number. By the {Lagrange Mean Value Theorem (LMVT)}, there exists some \( c \in (0,t) \) such that
\[
f'(c) = \frac{f(t) - f(0)}{t - 0} = \frac{f(t)}{t}.
\]
Taking absolute values on both sides, we get:
\[
|f'(c)| = \left| \frac{f(t)}{t} \right| = \frac{|f(t)|}{t}.
\]

Now suppose that \( f(t) \geq |f'(t)| \geq 0 \) for all \( t \in (0,1) \). Since \( f(t) \geq 0 \) and \( t \in (0,1) \), we multiply both sides of the inequality \( f(t) \geq \frac{|f(t)|}{t} \) by \( t > 0 \), yielding:
\[
f(t) \cdot t \geq |f(t)| \quad \Rightarrow \quad f(t) \cdot t \geq f(t) \quad \text{(since \( f(t) \geq 0 \))}.
\]

Subtracting \( f(t) \) from both sides:
\[
f(t)(t - 1) \geq 0.
\]

Now, since \( t \in (0,1) \), we have \( t - 1 < 0 \). Therefore, in order for \( f(t)(t - 1) \geq 0 \) to hold, we must have \( f(t) \leq 0 \).

But this contradicts the earlier assumption that \( f(t) \geq |f'(t)| \geq 0 \), which implies \( f(t) \leq 0 \). But f(t) can't be negative also . Hence the only possibility is:
\[

Click to expand$(1 + x)^n = \sum_{k = 0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^k$ . Differentiating both sides, $n(1 + x)^{n-1} = \sum_{k = 1}^{n} k \binom{n}{k} x^{k-1}$ . Setting $x = 1$ gives the required result.
Combo SolutionWe choose a committee of arbitrary size with a leader from a group of $n$ people. One way to do this is $n \cdot 2^{n-1}$ , where the first $n$ indicates the leader and the power of $2$ indicates choosing a subset of the rest. Another way to count it is to sum the possibilities over all possible sizes of the committee. stem_md:
There are 1000 doors  $D_1, D_2, . . . , D_{1000}$  and 1000 persons  $P_1, P_2, . . . , P_{1000}$ .
Initially all the doors were closed. Person  $P_1$  goes and opens all the doors.
Then person  $P_2$  closes door  $D_2, D_4, . . . , D_{1000}$   and leaves the odd numbered doors open. Next  $P_3$  changes the state of every third door, that
is,  $D_3, D_6, . . . , D_{999}$  . (For instance,  $P_3$  closes the open door  $D_3$  and opens
the closed door D6, and so on). Similarly,  $P_m$  changes the state of the
the doors  $D_m, D_{2m}, D_{3m}, . . . , D_{nm}, . . .$  while leaving the other doors untouched. Finally,  $P_{1000}$  opens  $D_{1000}$  if it was closed or closes it if it were
open. At the end, how many doors will remain open?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>It is not difficult to see that for any  $i,j \in \{1,2,3,\ldots,1000\},$  the person  $P_i$  will open the door  $D_j$  during their turn if and only if  $i$  divides  $j.$ Hence, for any particular  $k \in \{1,2,3,\ldots,1000\},$  the door  $D_k$  will be opened  $d(k)$  times where  $d(k)$  is the number of positive divisors of  $k.$ For that door to be open after all  $1000$  people have taken their turns, its state would have had to change an odd number of times since all doors began in their closed states. Hence,  $d(k)$  must be odd.

It is well-known that if  $k$  is a positive integer,  $d(k)$  is odd if and only if  $k$  is a perfect square, so we wish to find the number of perfect squares in the range  $\{1,2,3,\ldots,1000\}.$ This is just   $$ \left\lfloor \sqrt{1000} \right\rfloor = \boxed{31}. $$    $\square$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2013 MTRP Senior/3234028.json

stem_md: Let n be an integer such that if d | n then d + 1 | n + 1. Show that n is a prime number.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We want to show that  $x \mid n$  but  $x+1$  does not divide  $n+1$ .
Now, $n+1 = xy + 1$  $= (x + 1)y - y +1$ .
So  $n + 1 \equiv (1-y) \pmod{x+1}$ .
Next,  $1-y <0$  and  $(1-y) + (x + 1) = x - y + 2 > 0$ . 
Together, these imply that $(1 - y)$  is not equivalent to  $(x+1) \pmod{x+1}$  and so $(d+1)$  does not divide  $n+1$ .</details>

stem_md:
Let N = {1, 2, . . . , n} be a set of elements called voters. Let C = {S : S  $\subseteq$  N} be the power set of N. Members of C are called coalitions. Let f be a function from C to {0, 1}. A coalition S  $\subseteq$  N is said to be winning if f(S) = 1; it is said to be losing if f(S) = 0. Such a function is called a voting game if the following conditions hold:
(a) N is a wining coalition.
(b) The empty set  $\Phi$  is a losing coalition.
(c) If S is a winning coalition and S  $\subseteq$  S' is also winning.
(d) If both S and S' are winning then S  $\cap$  S'  $\neq$   $\Phi$ , i.e S and S' have a
common voter.
Show that the maximum number of winning coalitions of a voting game
is  $2^{n-1}$ . Also find such a voting game.
solution_md:
<details><summary>'Solution'</summary>Maximum # proof: there are  $2^n$  subsets of N. Now, pair up each subset with its complement. By condition d, there is at most 1 winning coalition in each pair (or else the two winning coalitions in the pair have no common element, contradiction), hence the maximum number is  $\frac{2^n}{2} = 2^{n-1}$ .

For its existence, consider all subsets that contain the element  $1$  to be winning, and otherwise losing.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2013 MTRP Senior/3234036.json

stem_md: Write 11 numbers on a sheet of paper six zeros and five ones. Perform the following operation 10 times: cross out any two numbers, and if they were equal, write another zero on the board. If they were not equal, write a one. Show that no matter which numbers are chosen at each step, the nal number on the board will be a one.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>First, we note that we will arrive at a single number in a finite number of operations because the number of numbers on the board is a strictly decreasing monovariant (as every operation exchanges  $2$  numbers for  $1$ ).

Then, we claim that the parity of the sum of the numbers on the board remains invariant under the given operation. We prove this by considering all possible number exchanges:**(i)** If two  $1$ 's are replaced by a  $0,$  the sum goes down by  $2,$  thus maintaining the parity.**(ii)** If two  $0$ 's are replaced by a  $0,$  the sum stays the same, thus maintaining the parity.**(iii)** If a  $1$  and a  $0$  are replaced by a  $1,$  the sum stays the same, thus maintaining the parity.

Since the sum of the numbers in the beginning is   $$ 6\cdot0+5\cdot1=0+5=5, $$   which is odd, it follows that the parity of the final sum is also odd, which can only be true if the final number is  $1.$   $\square$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2013 MTRP Senior/3234037.json

stem_md: Suppose 51 numbers are chosen from 1, 2, 3, ..., 99, 100. Show that there are two such that one divides the other.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>Let us define the sets  $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_{50}$  such that   $$ S_i = \left\{ x \mid x \in \{1,2,3,\ldots,100\}, \frac{x}{2^{\nu_2 (x)}}= 2i-1\right\} \ \forall \ i \in\{1,2,3,\ldots,50\}. $$  In other words, we split the numbers from  $1$  to  $100$  into  $50$  sets based on what number remains when you divide them by as many powers of  $2$  as possible.

Note that if some two distinct numbers  $x_1, x_2 \in \{1,2,3,\ldots,100\}$  both belong to some  $S_k$  where  $k \in \{1,2,3,\ldots,50\},$  then we can write   $$ x_1 = (2k-1) \cdot 2^{\nu_2(x_1)}, x_2 = (2k-1) \cdot 2^{\nu_2(x_2)}, $$   and thus one will clearly divide the other.

By the Pigeonhole Principle, if  $51$  numbers are chosen from  $\{1,2,3,\ldots,100\},$  then there will be  $2$  that both belong to the same  $S_i,$  so we are done.  $\square$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2013 MTRP Senior/3234038.json

If  $A_i=\frac{x-a_i}{|x-a_i|}$ ,  $i=1,2,\cdots,n$  for  $n$  numbers  $a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_m<\cdots<a_n,$  then  $\lim \limits_{x\to a_m}\Big(A_1A_2\cdots A_n\Big)=?$ [list=1]
[*]  $(-1)^{m-1}$ [*]  $(-1)^m$ [*]  $1$ [*] None of these
[/list]
solution_md: $\definecolor{A}{RGB}{0,90,255}\color{A}\fbox{Answer}\ 4.\text{ None of these}$ $\definecolor{A}{RGB}{0,90,255}\color{A}\fbox{Solution}$ $$ \lim \limits_{x\to a_m^+}A_m=\lim \limits_{x\to a_m^+}\frac{x-a_m}{|x-a_m|}=\lim \limits_{x\to a_m^+}\frac{x-a_m}{x-a_m}=1, $$ $$ \lim \limits_{x\to a_m^-}A_m=\lim \limits_{x\to a_m^-}\frac{x-a_m}{|x-a_m|}=\lim \limits_{x\to a_m^+}\frac{x-a_m}{-x+a_m}=-1 $$ so there is no $$ \lim \limits_{x\to a_m}A_m. $$ Functions $A_1,A_2,...,A_{m-1},A_{m+1},...,A_n$ have their limits at $a_m$ equal to $1$ or $-1$ . Therefore $\lim \limits_{x\to a_m}\Big(A_1A_2\cdots A_n\Big)$ doesn't exist. #1767

stem_md:
Let  $A C$  and  $C E$  be perpendicular line segments, each of length  $18 .$  Suppose  $B$  and  $D$  are the midpoints of  $A C$  and  $C E$  respectively. If  $F$  be the point of intersection of  $E B$  and  $A D,$  then the area of  $\triangle B D F$  is?

[list=1]
[*]  $27\sqrt{2}$ [*]  $18\sqrt{2}$ [*] 13.5
[*] 18
[/list]
solution_md:
Fortunately, this question can be easily barybashed :)

Let  $\triangle ACE$  be our reference triangle. Notice that  $F$  is the centroid. Hence, we can just spit out the coordinates:  $C=(1,0,0),A=(0,1,0),E=(0,0,1),B=(\tfrac 12,\tfrac 12,0),D=(\tfrac 12,0,\tfrac 12),F=(\tfrac 13,\tfrac 13,\tfrac 13)$ . So the area of  $\triangle BFD$  is  $\frac{1}{12}*\frac{18^2}2=\frac{27}2=13.5$  so pick option  $3$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2015 Mathematical Talent Reward Programme/2277498.json

[*] 360
[*] 364
[*] 365
[*] 366

solution_md:
Every element can either go into  $A, B$  or null.  $\Rightarrow$  Every element has 3 choices.
So, total number of choices for all the elements  $= 3^6$ .
Again, as  $(A, B)$  is an unordered pair, so, we mustn't count the repetitions.
Repetitions will occur only when,  $A, B$  are non-empty.
There are  $(3^6 - 1)$  such ordered pairs.  $\Rightarrow$  the number of unordered pairs for non-empty  $A, B$  =  $\frac{(3^6 - 1)}{2}$ .
Hence, total number of such unordered pairs  $= (\frac{(3^6 - 1)}{2} + 1) = (364 + 1) = 365$ .**Ans.** 3. 365.

stem_md:
Define  $f(x)=\max \{\sin x, \cos x\} .$  Find at how many points in  $(-2 \pi, 2 \pi), f(x)$  is not differentiable?
[list=1]
[*] 0
[*] 2
[*] 4
[*]  $\infty$ [/list]
solution_md:
The answer is the number of solutions to  $\sin x = \cos x$  in the interval  $(-2\pi, 2\pi)$ . It's clear that if some  $x$  does not satisfy this condition, then  $x$  lies entirely on either  $\sin$  or  $\cos$ , so it is differentiable. 

Now let  $x$  be a number that satisfies this condition. Then treating  $x$  as on  $\sin x$ , the slope of the tangent is  $\cos x$ . But treating  $x$  as on  $\cos x$ , the slope of the tangent is  $-\sin x$ . To be differentiable, these slopes should be equal, i.e.  $-\sin x = \cos x$ . But  $\sin x = \cos x$ , contradiction. (One can check that if  $\cos x = 0$ , then  $\sin x \neq \cos x$ .)

Hence we need to find the number of points such that  $\sin x = \cos x$ . But  $\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1$ , so  $\sin x = \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ . It's now clear that there are  $\boxed{4}$  solutions:  $-\tfrac{7\pi}{4}$ ,  $-\tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ ,  $\tfrac{\pi}{4}$ ,  $\tfrac{5\pi}{4}$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2015 Mathematical Talent Reward Programme/2277541.json

stem_md:
$z=x+i y$  where  $x$  and  $y$  are two real numbers. Find the locus of the point  $(x, y)$  in the plane, for which  $\frac{z+i}{z-i}$  is purely imaginary (that is, it is of the form  $i b$  where  $b$  is a real number). [Here,  $i=\sqrt{-1}$ [list=1]
[*] A straight line
[*] A circle
[*] A parabole
[*] None of these
[/list]
solution_md: If  $\frac{z + i}{z - i}$  has to be a pure imaginary number, then we must have  $\frac{z + i}{z - i} = -\overline{\left(\frac{z + i}{z - i}\right)}$ , or equivalently,  $\frac{z + i}{z - i} = -\frac{\bar z - i}{\bar z + i} \Rightarrow (z + i)(\bar z + i) = -(z - i)(\bar z - i) \Rightarrow |z|^2 - 1 + i(z + \bar z) = -(|z|^2 - 1) + i(z + \bar z) \Rightarrow |z|^2 = 1$ , which means that the locus of  $z$  is the unit circle.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2015 Mathematical Talent Reward Programme/2277546.json

stem_md: Let  $a$  be the smallest and  $A$  the largest of  $n$  distinct positive integers. Prove that the least common multiple of these numbers is greater than or equal to  $n a$  and that the greatest common divisor is less than or equal to  $\frac{A}{n}$
solution_md:
Let   $\langle x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \rangle$  be a sequence of  $n$  distinct positive integers where  $x_1<x_2<\ldots<x_n$ . So here  $a=x_1$  and  $A=x_n$ . We see that,
\[x_1\cdot x_2\cdots x_n \geq x_1 \cdot x_n = a \cdot A\]
for  $n \geq 2$ . We also see that 
\[gcd(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\;|\;gcd(a,A)\]
Hence we may write that
\[gcd(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \leq gcd(a,A)\]
Using this information in the first inequality we see that 
\begin{align*}
    & x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n \geq a,A
    \Rightarrow& gcd(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n)\;lcm(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n) \geq gcd(a,A)\;lcm(a,A)
    \Rightarrow& gcd(a,A)\;lcm(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n) \geq &gcd(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n)\;lcm(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n) \geq gcd(a,A)\;lcm(a,A)
    \Rightarrow& lcm(x_1,x_2,\cdots,x_n) \geq lcm(a,A)
\end{align*}
So we are left to show that
\[gcd(a,A) \leq \frac{A}{n}\]
\[lcm(a,A) \geq an\]
We start with the first one. We need to find maximum possible value of  $gcd(a,A)$ . As  $a<A$  so the maximum gcd is possible only when  $A$  is some multiple of  $a$ . So let  $A=ak$  for some  $k > 1$ . Now we notice that  $k$  has a minimum value, which we find when we let the series  $\langle x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \rangle$  = $\langle a,2a,\ldots,na \rangle$ . Hence we notice that the minimum value of  $k$  is  $n$ . Hence 
\[k \geq n\]
Using this we get
\[gcd(a,A) = gcd(a,ak) = a = \frac{A}{k} \leq \frac{A}{n}\]
So the maximum value of  $gcd(a,A)$  is lesser or equal to  $\frac{A}{n}$ . Hence the following inequality does satisfy,
\[gcd(a,A) \leq \frac{A}{n}\]
Now the second inequality. We already have put  $A=ak$ . Using this in the second inequality, because more common factors  $A$  has with  $a$  with can find the minimum value of the inequality, we get,
\[lcm(a,A) = lcm(a,ak) = ak \geq an\]
As the minimum value is greater or equal to  $an$ , hence the following inequality follows,
\[lcm(a,A) \geq an\]
Hence proved.

In the following figure, the bigger wheel has circumference  $12$ m and the inscribed wheel has circumference  $8 $ m.  $P_{1}$  denotes a point on the bigger wheel and  $P_{2}$  denotes a point on the smaller wheel. Initially  $P_{1}$  and  $P_{2}$  coincide as in the figure. Now we roll the wheels on a smooth surface and the smaller wheel also rolls in the bigger wheel smoothly. What distance does the bigger wheel have to roll so that the points will be together again?

**Attachments:**

![Screenshot_2020-09-22-09-32-25-1.png](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/9/d/f77f25c35d0487996fabe9c60375615d5f9c73.png)
solution_md: <details><summary>sol????</summary>$P_1$  goes back to its original spot when it travels the length of the circumference of the circle, which is every  $8$  meters.  $P_2$  also goes back to its spot every  $12$  meters. (They roll at the same rate, so)... So, the distance until they are together again is the LCM of  $8$  and  $12$  (meters).  $8=2^3$ , and  $12=2^2\cdot 3$ , so  $\text{LCM}(8,12)=2^3\cdot 3=24$ . Therefore, the outer wheel must roll  $24$  meters before they coincide again???</details>

Let  $f$  be a function satisfying  $f(x+y+z)=f(x)+f(y)+f(z)$  for all integers  $x$ ,  $y$ ,  $z$ . Suppose  $f(1)=1$ ,  $f(2)=2$ . Then  $\lim \limits_{n\to \infty} \frac{1}{n^3} \sum \limits_{r=1}^n 4rf(3r)$  equals
[list=1]
[*] 4
[*] 6
[*] 12
[*] 24
[/list]
solution_md: $f(x+y+z)=f(x)+f(y)+f(z),x,y,z\in \mathbb{N}\Rightarrow f(n)=a,f(1)=1\Rightarrow f(n)=n$   $\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{1}{{{n}^{3}}}\sum\limits_{r=1}^{n}{4}rf(3r)=\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{12}{{{n}^{3}}}\sum\limits_{r=1}^{n}{{{r}^{2}}}=\underset{n\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{12n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6{{n}^{3}}}=4$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2016 Mathematical Talent Reward Programme/2128978.json

solution_md: For completion:  $$ 2\cdot\textrm{Re}\left(\frac{z}{1-z^2}\right)=\frac{z}{1-z^2}+\overline{\frac{z}{1-z^2}}=\frac{z-\bar{z}+\bar{z}-z}{(1-z^2)(1-\overline{z}^2)}=0. $$

stem_md:
There are 168 primes below 1000. Then sum of all primes below 1000 is 
[list=1]
[*] 11555
[*] 76127
[*] 57298
[*] 81722
[/list]
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution by elimination</summary>Note that all primes greater than  $2$  are odd, so there are 167 odd primes below 1000 and an even prime. Therefore, their sum must be odd, which eliminates the choices 3 and 4. Moreover,  $\frac{168 \cdot 169}{2}>11555$  by some calculations so the sum of the first 168 primes must be greater than  $11555$  and hence we cross out the  $1^{st}$  choice. Hence, the sum of all primes below 1000 is  $\boxed{76127}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/India Contests/Mathematics Talent Reward Programme (MTRP)/2016 Mathematical Talent Reward Programme/2128987.json

Number of solutions of the equation  $3^x+4^x=8^x$  in reals is
[list=1]
[*] 0
[*] 1
[*] 2
[*]  $\infty$ [/list]
solution_md: We have  ${{3}^{x}}+{{4}^{x}}={{8}^{x}}\Leftrightarrow {{\left( \frac{3}{8} \right)}^{x}}+{{\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)}^{x}}=1$ , the LHS it is descreasing, the RHS constant, so we have maximum  $1$  solution, and if  $f(x)={{\left( \frac{3}{8} \right)}^{x}}+{{\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)}^{x}}-1\Rightarrow f(0)f(1)<0$  so indeed we have only one solution.
